title: SYSK Selects: How Coral Reefs Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2012 episode on coral reefs. Josh introduces it as a pick from March 2012 and the hosts cover how corals are living carnivorous animals (polyps) in a symbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae algae, how limestone skeletons build reefs, reproduction and growth rates, coral sand and coralline algae, the three reef types (fringing, barrier, atoll) and their zones (back, crest, fore reef, buttress zone), the Great Barrier Reef, threats such as bleaching, blast and cyanide fishing, runoff, and mining, economic value of reefs, and ways to help. The episode closes with listener mail from Diane Bowls about a village library in Malawi.

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, a 2012 episode on coral reefs. The hosts banter about vitamins and Josh's scuba certification at Isla Mujeres near Cozumel, then introduce the topic.

segments.title: Coral polyps, carnivores and the algae partnership
segments.summary: Corals are animals, not plants: polyps in the phylum Cnidaria that use stinging nematocysts to catch prey and are sessile. They host zooxanthellae algae that photosynthesize and share energy for the polyp, which in turn provides shelter.

segments.title: How reefs grow: limestone, reproduction and growth rates
segments.summary: Polyps secrete calcium carbonate limestone cups that accumulate into colonies and reefs, joined by a tissue called the coenosarc. Corals reproduce sexually or asexually by cloning. Growth is slow, up to about 10 cm (3.9 inches) a year in ideal conditions, so reefs take thousands of years to build.

segments.title: Ideal conditions for coral
segments.summary: Reef-building corals need warm, clear, sunlit equatorial waters, roughly between 73.4 and 84.2 degrees Fahrenheit (about 23 to 29 C), and nutrient-poor water. Nutrients attract competition and filter sunlight.

segments.title: Coral sand and coralline algae repair
segments.summary: Waves and fish break coral into coral sand, which fills gaps and is then cemented by coralline algae. Mining coral sand for bricks, cement and fill removes this natural repair, threatening reefs. An estimate says a large share of the world's reefs could be gone within a few decades.

segments.title: Types of reefs and reef zones
segments.summary: Three reef types are described: fringing reefs attached to land, barrier reefs separated from land by a gap of water, and atolls formed around a sunken island or volcano. Reef zones include the back reef, the crest, the fore reef, and the buttress zone, where channels funnel waves back out to sea.

segments.title: The Great Barrier Reef and the largest living structure
segments.summary: The Great Barrier Reef is described as the largest living structure on the planet, visible from space, with thousands of reefs and about 18,000 miles of reef edge. It has many coral and fish species, was made a national marine park in 1975 and a World Heritage Site later; about one percent is research-only. The hosts mention a large Oregon fungus as a comparison.

segments.title: Threats to coral reefs
segments.summary: Natural threats include hurricanes and El Nino, plus coral bleaching when warming of about one degree drives out the algae. Predators such as crabs, worms, snails and parrotfish also eat polyps. Human threats include blast fishing with dynamite, cyanide fishing, overfishing, runoff of pollutants and sewage that increase nutrients, and mining of coral sand. About 10 percent of reefs are beyond recovery.

segments.title: Ways to help and the economic value of reefs
segments.summary: Listeners can adopt a reef through adopt.nature.org, lobby lawmakers on fishing oversight, boycott products from countries using blast fishing, and avoid taking coral when diving. Reefs are economically valuable: Florida reefs are valued at about 8.5 billion dollars with many jobs, and reefs bring in about 9.6 billion dollars a year from tourism and recreation worldwide.
